title: CAP Theorem
description: How a partitioned system chooses between answering and staying consistent, and how Dynamo and Spanner made opposite choices.
concept: The CAP theorem says that when a network partition splits a distributed system, each side can either keep answering (availability) or refuse to answer stale or conflicting data (consistency), but not both. Partitions are a fact of networks, so the real choice is what to do during one: Dynamo-style systems stay available and reconcile divergent copies afterwards, while Spanner-style systems stay consistent and make the losing side wait. CAP is a per-operation trade-off between how fresh an answer must be and how often the system must answer at all, so it gets decided for each kind of data and never once for the whole system.

points: When a network partition splits a system, each side can keep answering or refuse stale data, but not both.
Partitions are a fact of networks, so the real choice is what to do during one, and it is decided for each kind of data.
Amazon's Dynamo starts from never rejecting a write and derives quorums, hinted handoff and reconciliation from that rule.
Google's Spanner keeps strong consistency across the globe by paying a bounded latency and engineering the clock.

figures.label: Amazon's example SLA asks for 99.9% of requests within 300 ms
TrueTime clock uncertainty is 1 to 7 ms, which a transaction waits out

prerequisiteReasons.replication: CAP takes from replication the picture of several copies of one key that can end up on opposite sides of a network split.
prerequisiteReasons.sharding: CAP takes from sharding the fact that data lives on many machines joined by a network, which is where partitions come from.

why.outcome: After this you can explain why a partitioned system must give up either consistency or availability, and why partition tolerance is not optional.
why.body:
Spread data across machines and the network between them will, sometimes, break: a switch fails, a link saturates, a datacenter is cut off. That is a partition, and in a distributed system it is a when, not an if. So partition tolerance is the condition you are forced to design under, and you cannot trade it away like a third option.

Given a partition, a node that cannot reach its peers faces one question: answer anyway, or refuse? If it answers, it might serve data that another side has already changed, or accept a write the other side never sees, which breaks consistency but keeps availability. If it refuses until it can confirm with its peers, it stays consistent but becomes unavailable to that client. That is CAP: during a partition you choose consistency or availability, because you cannot have both at once. When there is no partition, a good system gives you both.

mentalModel.outcome: After this you can picture a partition splitting a system and reason about each side's choice.
mentalModel.body:
Picture three replicas of one key, and a network split that puts one replica on the far side of a partition from a client's two others. The client writes to the two it can reach. The third never hears the write.

Now another client, on the far side, reads that same key from the lone replica. The system has two options. The consistent (CP) option: the lone replica refuses, because it cannot confirm it has the latest value, so that client is unavailable until the partition heals. The available (AP) option: the lone replica answers with what it has, which is stale, and the two sides are reconciled later when they can talk again. Neither is wrong; they are different promises. The quorum is the usual dial: require a write to reach W replicas and a read to reach R, and if R plus W is greater than N, every read set overlaps the latest acknowledged write set. That overlap is necessary but not sufficient for strong consistency, and it needs strict quorums: a sloppy quorum, which accepts writes on stand-in nodes, does not give it. The cost of the overlap is needing more replicas reachable to answer.

howItWorks.outcome: After this you can walk through how a quorum system turns the CAP choice into tunable R and W values and what happens when a partition hits.

steps.explanation: Every key is stored on N replicas, chosen by the hashing scheme. N sets how many machines could serve or must agree.
A write must be acknowledged by W replicas; a read must gather R. These are dials: higher values mean fresher data but more machines must be reachable to answer.

If R plus W is greater than N, every read set overlaps every write set, so a read always includes a replica that has the latest acknowledged write. This is necessary but not sufficient for strong consistency: concurrent writes still need ordering or reconciliation. It also needs strict quorums, because a sloppy quorum, which accepts writes on stand-in nodes outside the usual N, does not give the overlap.
Lower R and W (so R plus W is at most N) let reads and writes succeed with fewer replicas, so the system keeps answering during a partition, at the risk of returning stale data.

During a partition a CP system refuses operations it cannot make safe (a side without a quorum stops answering); an AP system accepts them on whatever replicas are reachable and records that versions have diverged.
An AP system must later merge the divergent versions, by last-write-wins, by vector clocks that detect concurrent edits, or by application logic such as merging two shopping carts.

When R plus W exceeds N the read and write sets overlap (consistent); smaller R and W keep the system answering during a partition (available) and diverged versions are reconciled later.</title><defs><marker id="dg-c-cap-how-a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M1,1 L9,5 L1,9" class="dg-head"/></marker></defs><text x="280" y="22" class="dg-note" text-anchor="middle">N = 3 replicas of one key</text><rect x="90" y="40" width="110" height="40" class="dg-box"/><text x="145" y="64.5" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">replica A</text><rect x="225" y="40" width="110" height="40" class="dg-box"/><text x="280" y="64.5" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">replica B</text><rect x="360" y="40" width="110" height="40" class="dg-box"/><text x="415" y="64.5" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">replica C</text><rect x="70" y="120" width="200" height="44" class="dg-box dg-accent"/><text x="170" y="140" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">W = 2 (write set)</text><text x="170" y="157" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">A, B</text><rect x="290" y="120" width="200" height="44" class="dg-box dg-accent"/><text x="390" y="140" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">R = 2 (read set)</text><text x="390" y="157" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">B, C</text><path d="M170,120 L150,84" class="dg-line" marker-end="url(#dg-c-cap-how-a)"/><path d="M180,120 L280,84" class="dg-line" marker-end="url(#dg-c-cap-how-a)"/><path d="M380,120 L290,84" class="dg-line" marker-end="url(#dg-c-cap-how-a)"/><path d="M400,120 L415,84" class="dg-line" marker-end="url(#dg-c-cap-how-a)"/><text x="280" y="210" class="dg-note" text-anchor="middle">R + W = 4 > N = 3, so the sets overlap at B: the read sees the write</text><text x="280" y="232" class="dg-note" text-anchor="middle">lower R + W keeps answering in a partition; diverged copies are merged later</text></svg>

workedExample.outcome: After this you can trace one key through a partition under both an available and a consistent policy, and see where staleness or a refusal appears.

steps.explanation: A user's profile is stored on replicas A, B and C (N = 3). Normally reads and writes touch a quorum of two, so R plus W is 4, greater than 3, and every read overlaps the latest acknowledged write. That overlap is necessary but not sufficient for strong consistency, and it holds only while writes go to the key's own replicas, not to stand-ins as in a sloppy quorum.
A network fault cuts C off from A and B. A and B can still reach each other; C is alone.
A client on C's side updates the profile. With W = 1, C accepts it and answers reads, so C's side stays up but now disagrees with A and B. A client on the A, B side reads a stale profile.
With W = 2 and R = 2, C cannot gather a quorum alone, so writes and reads on C's side are refused. The data never diverges, but C's clients are unavailable until the partition heals.

Under the available policy, A, B and C now hold different versions. Vector clocks show the edits were concurrent, so the system either picks last-write-wins or hands both versions to the application to merge.

steps.step: Choose per data, not per system
steps.explanation: A shopping cart can merge, so availability is fine. An account balance cannot tolerate two truths, so it wants the consistent policy. The same cluster can run both by setting R and W per operation.

lesson.mistakesOutcome: After this you can avoid three misreadings of CAP.
lesson.checkOutcome: After this you can tell whether you understood the concept before reading the posts.

quiz.question: What does the CAP theorem actually force you to choose between?
options: Speed and correctness, which no distributed system can ever have together, with or without a partition
Consistency and availability, but only while a network partition is happening
Consistency, availability, and partition tolerance, picking any two at all times
quiz.why: Partitions are unavoidable, so the real trade-off is what a node does during one: answer (available) or refuse to serve unsafe data (consistent). With no partition you can have both.
wrong: CAP is about consistency versus availability under partitions, not a general speed-versus-correctness rule.
The popular "pick two of three" phrasing is misleading: partition tolerance is not optional on a real network, so the choice is really consistency versus availability during a partition.

quiz.question: Why can't you simply trade away partition tolerance to keep both consistency and availability?
options: Because networks fail, so partitions happen whether or not you plan for them
Because partition tolerance is the most valuable of the three
Because dropping it would make the system slower
quiz.why: A partition is a physical event on the network, not a design option; the system only gets to decide how it behaves when one occurs.
wrong: Ranking the three does not help: a partition is a fact of the network that you cannot opt out of.
Dropping partition tolerance is not even possible on a real network, so speed is beside the point.

quiz.question: A key is stored on N = 3 replicas with R = 2 and W = 2. What does R + W > N buy you?
options: Strong consistency on its own, with no other conditions needed at all, even when writes land on stand-in replicas
The ability to answer even when two replicas are unreachable
Reads that overlap the latest acknowledged write, necessary but not sufficient for strong consistency
quiz.why: With R + W greater than N, every read quorum shares at least one replica with every write quorum, so a read always includes a replica that holds the latest acknowledged write. That is necessary but not sufficient for strong consistency: concurrent writes still need ordering, and a sloppy quorum, which accepts writes on stand-in nodes outside the usual N, does not give the overlap at all.
wrong: R + W > N is necessary but not sufficient: concurrent writes and sloppy quorums, which accept writes on stand-in nodes, can still leave reads stale or conflicting.
Needing a quorum of 2 means it cannot answer when two of three are unreachable; that is the availability cost.

quiz.question: During a partition, an AP (available) system accepts writes on both sides. What must it do once the partition heals?
options: Nothing, because the versions are guaranteed identical once the network is restored
Delete every write made during the partition and restart both sides from the last shared state
Reconcile the diverged versions, by last-write-wins, vector clocks, or application merge
quiz.why: Both sides accepted independent writes, so the copies disagree and must be merged; vector clocks detect which edits were concurrent.
wrong: Each side took writes the other never saw, so they are not identical; that is the whole cost of staying available.
Throwing away partition-time writes would lose acknowledged data, which defeats accepting them in the first place.

quiz.question: When is it right to choose the consistent (CP) policy for a piece of data?
options: When two conflicting truths would be dangerous, like an account balance
Always, because consistency is strictly better than availability in every system
When the data can be merged safely, like a shopping cart
quiz.why: Data that must never disagree, such as a balance, is worth refusing service during a partition rather than risking divergence.
wrong: Consistency costs availability during partitions, so it is not strictly better; mergeable data is fine to keep available.
Mergeable data like a cart is the case for staying available, not for choosing consistency.

quiz.question: What is the most accurate way to apply CAP in a real system?
options: Label the whole database as CP or AP once and for all
Choose per operation, since R and W can be set differently for different data
Avoid partitions so CAP never applies
quiz.why: The same cluster can serve a mergeable, available workload and a must-be-correct, consistent one by tuning R and W per request.
wrong: A single global label is too coarse; different data in the same store wants different trade-offs.
Partitions cannot be avoided on a real network, so you must decide behaviour for when they happen.

lesson.postsOutcome: After this you can describe two production systems that made opposite CAP choices and how each paid for it.
lesson.differOutcome: After this you can explain why Dynamo stayed available and Spanner stayed consistent, and what each spent to do so.
lesson.exercisesOutcome: After this you can set a quorum for a given need, design consistency for a mixed workload, and reason about a global system under partitions.

exercises.prompt: A product catalogue is read constantly and updated rarely, and must stay readable even if a replica or two is unreachable. It is stored on N = 3 replicas. Pick R and W and justify them.
exercises.answer: Favour availability for reads: R = 1 (a read answers from any one replica) and W = 2 or 3 so writes are durable. Reads stay available even when replicas are down, and because the catalogue changes rarely, brief staleness after an update is acceptable and converges quickly. If you need a read to see the latest write, raise R so R + W is greater than 3.
exercises.tradeoffs: R = 1 can return a slightly stale entry just after an update. Higher W makes writes slower and need more replicas up, but writes are rare here, so that is cheap.
wrongAnswers: R = 3 for every read, which makes reads fail whenever any replica is down.
W = 1 and R = 1, risking lost or unseen writes with no overlap.
Treating the catalogue as if it needed account-balance consistency.

exercises.prompt: One service stores both shopping carts (mergeable) and payment balances (must never disagree) in the same key-value cluster. Design the consistency so each behaves correctly during a partition.
exercises.answer: Set the policy per key class. Carts use low R and W (stay available; on heal, merge the two cart versions with application logic or vector clocks), so a partition never blocks shopping. Balances use R + W greater than N (a quorum), so a side without a quorum refuses the operation during a partition rather than let two balances diverge. The cluster is neither globally AP nor CP; the data decides.
exercises.tradeoffs: Carts can briefly show a stale or merged state; that is acceptable. Balances become unavailable to a partitioned minority, which is the correct price for never double-spending. You must classify every key type deliberately.
wrongAnswers: One global consistency level for the whole cluster.
Making balances available and merging them like carts, risking lost money.
Making carts strongly consistent, so a partition blocks checkout needlessly.

exercises.prompt: You need a globally distributed database that stays strongly consistent across continents. Partitions and high cross-region latency are givens. What are you signing up for, and how do systems make it bearable?
exercises.answer: Choosing consistency across a wide area means some operations must wait for agreement among replicas in distant regions, so write latency includes a cross-region round trip, and a partitioned minority region cannot commit. Systems make it bearable by keeping a majority quorum reachable (so a single region's loss does not stop writes), placing data close to its users, and shrinking the window they must wait: Spanner uses tightly synchronised clocks (TrueTime) to bound uncertainty and commit with a short wait rather than a long coordination round for reads.
exercises.tradeoffs: Strong global consistency costs latency and makes a cut-off region read-only or down; the alternative, staying available, would mean reconciling conflicting writes across continents, which is often worse for the data in question.
wrongAnswers: Assuming you can have low latency, global strong consistency, and full partition availability at once.
Putting all replicas in one region to dodge the problem, losing global availability.
Ignoring clock skew when ordering writes across regions.

next.outcome: After this you can choose the next topic that builds on CAP.
next.body: CAP sets up Consensus, where a majority of replicas agree on one order of events so a system can stay consistent and available as long as a quorum survives. It also underlies Distributed transactions, which need agreement across shards, and it revisits Replication and Sharding, the mechanisms a partition acts on.

posts.title: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store
posts.ageNote: This is a research paper, not a company blog post: the 2007 SOSP paper. It is here for a fundamental that has not changed: how a system deliberately chooses availability over strong consistency and reconciles divergence afterwards. The DynamoDB product Amazon sells today has evolved well beyond this design and now offers strongly consistent reads, so treat the paper as the origin of the ideas, not a description of the current service.

digest.problem: Amazon's e-commerce platform needed storage for services that must give an "always-on" experience, such as the shopping cart, where even a brief inability to write loses sales and trust. Many of these services only need primary-key access, not relational queries. The team wanted a store that is always writable, scales incrementally, and keeps answering through the failures and partitions that are routine at Amazon's scale.
digest.constraints: Amazon states its service level agreements at the 99.9th percentile, not the mean. The paper's example is a response within 300 ms for 99.9% of requests at a peak load of 500 requests per second. Writes must never be rejected, even during failures. The design assumes commodity hardware that fails constantly and must tolerate partitions without an operator in the loop.

walkthrough.explanation: Keys are spread around a consistent hashing ring and each key is stored on N nodes that follow its position. The list of nodes responsible for a key is its preference list, which holds more than N nodes to cover failures, so adding or removing a node moves only a slice of the data.

walkthrough.step: Make it always writable with tunable quorums
walkthrough.explanation: The protocol has two configurable values, R and W, over N replicas, and the paper says they are usually set below N for better latency. The common configuration is (3, 2, 2). Raising W makes writes more durable but can reject them when fewer hosts are alive.

walkthrough.step: Keep writing during failures with a sloppy quorum
walkthrough.explanation: If a replica is unreachable, the write goes to the next healthy node on the ring with a hint; this hinted handoff lets writes succeed through partitions, and the hint is delivered back when the node returns.
Each version carries a vector clock. On read, the system compares clocks: if one version descends from another it keeps the newer; if they are concurrent, it returns both as conflicts.

walkthrough.step: Reconcile conflicts, often in the application
walkthrough.explanation: Simple cases use last-write-wins, but Dynamo lets the application resolve, for example by merging the conflicting versions of a shopping cart into one unified cart so no added item is lost.
An anti-entropy process using Merkle trees compares replicas and heals differences, and read repair fixes stale replicas it notices during reads.

digest.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" role="img" aria-labelledby="dg-dynamo-t" class="dg"><title id="dg-dynamo-t">Dynamo: keys sit on a consistent hashing ring, each replicated to the next N nodes; writes use low W and are never rejected, going to the next healthy node with a hint during a partition; vector clocks detect concurrent versions, which the application reconciles (for example merging shopping carts).</title><defs><marker id="dg-dynamo-a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M1,1 L9,5 L1,9" class="dg-head"/></marker></defs><circle cx="150" cy="150" r="96" class="dg-box" fill="none"/><text x="150" y="44" class="dg-note" text-anchor="middle">consistent hashing ring</text><circle cx="150" cy="54" r="7" class="dg-box dg-accent"/><circle cx="241" cy="120" r="7" class="dg-box dg-accent"/><circle cx="206" cy="226" r="7" class="dg-box dg-accent"/><circle cx="94" cy="226" r="7" class="dg-box"/><circle cx="59" cy="120" r="7" class="dg-box"/><text x="150" y="150" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">key k</text><text x="150" y="168" class="dg-note" text-anchor="middle">N = 3 (rust)</text><rect x="330" y="60" width="210" height="40" class="dg-box"/><text x="435" y="84.5" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">write: low W, never rejected</text><rect x="330" y="120" width="210" height="40" class="dg-box"/><text x="435" y="138" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">partition: hinted handoff</text><text x="435" y="154" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">to next healthy node</text><rect x="330" y="180" width="210" height="52" class="dg-box"/><text x="435" y="200" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">concurrent versions:</text><text x="435" y="217" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">vector clocks, app merge</text><path d="M246,145 L330,110" class="dg-line" marker-end="url(#dg-dynamo-a)"/><text x="280" y="278" class="dg-note" text-anchor="middle">available first: answer now, reconcile later</text></svg>

numbers.meaning: The paper's example SLA, for a peak client load of 500 requests per second; Amazon measures SLAs at the 99.9th percentile rather than the mean
The common (N, R, W) configuration the paper reports for several Dynamo instances; R and W are usually set below N for better latency
The period over which the versions returned to the shopping cart service were profiled; 99.94% of requests saw exactly one version

tradeoffs.chosen: Availability and incremental scalability: an always-writable store with low quorums, sloppy quorum with hinted handoff, and conflict resolution pushed to read time and often to the application.
tradeoffs.rejected: Strong consistency and the simplicity of a single authoritative copy, which would make the system unavailable to a partitioned side.
tradeoffs.why: For the shopping cart and similar services, refusing a write during a partition is worse than briefly diverging, because the data can be merged. Dynamo therefore keeps answering and spends the cost later, in conflict reconciliation and in the complexity of vector clocks and anti-entropy.

digest.failures: The design is candid about its costs. The basic consistent hashing scheme gave uneven load and had to be refined. Vector clocks can grow with the number of nodes that touch a key, so their size must be bounded. Pushing conflict resolution to the application is powerful, but some developers do not want to write their own, so the data store can apply a simple policy such as last write wins instead.
digest.takeaways: CAP is a design input from the first day: Dynamo starts from "never reject a write" and derives quorums, hinted handoff and reconciliation from it. The lesson that outlived the specifics is that availability is bought with eventual consistency and a reconciliation strategy, and that the right strategy depends on the data, which is why Dynamo made R, W and conflict handling tunable.

posts.title: Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database
posts.ageNote: This is a research paper, not a company blog post: the 2012 OSDI paper. It is here for a fundamental that has not changed: how a system chooses strong consistency across the globe and engineers around partitions and clock uncertainty rather than giving up consistency. Cloud Spanner has grown since, but the TrueTime and commit-wait ideas the paper introduces are the point.

digest.problem: Google needed a database that scales across datacenters worldwide yet still offers strong, SQL-like semantics, including externally consistent transactions. Its advertising backend, F1, was moving off a manually sharded MySQL deployment that was painful to reshard and operate. The goal was global scale without giving up the consistency that application developers rely on.
digest.constraints: Spanner commits to external consistency (a global linearizable order of transactions), which, in our CAP framing (the paper does not use it), is the opposite stance from Dynamo. It runs across datacenters connected by wide-area links, so it must tolerate partitions while never serving an order of transactions that violates real time. It leans on replication by Paxos and on tightly controlled time.

walkthrough.step: Shard into directories, replicate by Paxos
walkthrough.explanation: Data is split into directories, the unit of placement, each replicated across datacenters by a Paxos group so a majority can make progress and the system can fail over between replicas automatically.

walkthrough.step: Give the system a trustworthy clock
walkthrough.explanation: TrueTime exposes time as an interval, not a point, built from GPS receivers and atomic clocks, and returns an uncertainty bound rather than pretending the clock is exact.
Over a poll interval, TrueTime's uncertainty ranges from about 1 to 7 ms, so the system knows the true time lies within a known, small window.

A transaction picks a commit timestamp and then waits out the uncertainty interval before releasing its result, which guarantees that any transaction that starts later gets a strictly later timestamp. This is how external consistency is enforced.
Transactions spanning Paxos groups use two-phase commit over those groups, with the Paxos leaders as participants, so a write across shards is atomic and ordered.
Read-only transactions can run at a timestamp on any replica that is sufficiently up to date, avoiding locks, so reads scale without a coordination round.

numbers.meaning: TrueTime's clock uncertainty over a poll interval; a transaction waits out this window to guarantee ordering
Paxos latency in the paper's one-replica latency experiments, where commit wait was about 5 ms
Network distance between datacenters in the measured configuration
Size of a directory, the unit of data placement, that the paper expects can be moved between Paxos groups in a few seconds (an expectation, not a measurement)

tradeoffs.chosen: Strong, external consistency at global scale: Paxos replication, two-phase commit across shards, and commit-wait against TrueTime so there is always one correct global order.
tradeoffs.rejected: The availability-first, eventually consistent approach, and the pretence that clocks are exact.
tradeoffs.why: Google judged that giving application developers strong consistency and SQL was worth paying latency for, because reasoning about an eventually consistent store across continents is harder than paying a bounded wait. Rather than drop consistency, Spanner shrinks the cost by making clock uncertainty small and known, so the commit-wait is short.

digest.failures: The honesty is in the costs it accepts. Commit-wait adds latency to writes, bounded by TrueTime's uncertainty, so the whole design depends on keeping that uncertainty small, which needs real GPS and atomic-clock hardware in every datacenter. Our reading, not stated in the paper: a partitioned minority of replicas cannot form a Paxos majority, so it cannot commit, which is the availability price of choosing consistency.
digest.takeaways: Spanner is the counterexample to "you must give up consistency to go distributed": you can keep strong consistency globally if you are willing to pay a bounded latency and engineer the clock. It shows the CAP choice depends on what you are willing to spend, since distribution alone does not force it, and that making the uncertainty window small and measurable is what makes the consistent choice affordable.

comparison:
Both papers face the same impossibility and both run at enormous scale, but they sit on opposite sides of the CAP choice, which is exactly why they belong together. Dynamo starts from "a write must never be rejected" and accepts eventual consistency; Spanner starts from "transactions must have one correct global order" and accepts added latency. Reading them in sequence is the clearest way to see that CAP is a decision you make.

Where they diverge is what each spends. Dynamo spends on reconciliation: vector clocks, sloppy quorums with hinted handoff, read repair, anti-entropy with Merkle trees, and application-level merges, all to keep answering during a partition and sort out divergence later. Spanner spends on coordination and hardware: Paxos majorities, two-phase commit across shards, and GPS plus atomic clocks feeding TrueTime so a short commit-wait can enforce order. Dynamo's partitioned side stays available but may be stale; Spanner's partitioned minority goes unavailable but is never wrong.

The evidence shows the price of each stance. Dynamo's goal is a 99.9th-percentile SLA of 300 ms with writes never rejected, and its complexity lives in conflict handling. Spanner's numbers are about the cost of agreement: Paxos latency around 9 ms in the paper's one-replica experiments and a TrueTime uncertainty of roughly 1 to 7 ms that every committing transaction waits out. Neither is the right answer in general; the right answer depends on whether the data can be merged, which is the real lesson under CAP.

glossary.definition: A break in the network that stops some nodes from reaching others, during which CAP forces a choice.
Every read sees the latest acknowledged write, as if there were one copy of the data.
Every request to a reachable, non-failed node gets a non-error response, even during a partition.
The system keeps operating despite dropped or delayed messages between nodes; on a real network this is mandatory.

N replicas per key; a write needs W acknowledgements and a read needs R. R + W > N makes every read set overlap the latest acknowledged write, which is necessary but not sufficient for strong consistency; sloppy quorums do not give the overlap.
With no new writes, all replicas converge to the same value in time; the available side of CAP relies on it.
Per-version counters that reveal whether one version descends from another or the two were written concurrently.
During a failure, a write goes to a stand-in node with a hint, which forwards it to the intended node on recovery.
A global order of transactions that respects real time: if one commits before another starts, it orders earlier.
Spanner's clock that returns time as a bounded interval, from GPS and atomic clocks, so uncertainty is known.
Waiting out the clock-uncertainty interval before releasing a transaction, so timestamps order correctly.

mistakes: Reading CAP as "pick any two of three". Partition tolerance is not optional on a real network, so the real choice is consistency versus availability only while a partition is happening; with no partition you can have both.

Treating a whole database as permanently CP or AP. The trade-off is really per operation: the same quorum store can serve mergeable data available and must-be-correct data consistent by setting R and W differently.

Assuming strong consistency across a wide area is free, or that eventual consistency means data is simply wrong. Consistency costs latency and minority availability; eventual consistency means converging after reconciliation, not never agreeing.
